screens.title: Advanced Testing Techniques and Test Networks
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how to test smart contract behavior beyond single-function unit checks. We'll focus on three practical areas: asserting event emissions so your front-end and indexers can rely on on-chain signals; building integration tests that exercise interactions between two or more contracts; and using Hardhat Network to simulate time, impersonate accounts, and debug with console logging. These capabilities help you catch bugs that unit tests miss: incorrect event arguments, approval mistakes, and time-dependent logic. You'll see concrete code examples: a Counter contract extended to emit events, Waffle assertions using the to. emit and withArgs matchers, and an integration test pattern for an ERC20 token and a TokenSale contract. We will also cover common mistakes like forgetting to use contract. connect(signer) or skipping event assertions. By the end, you'll understand how to structure tests that mirror real-world flows and how to use Hardhat's network features to reproduce scenarios that are hard to recreate on public testnets. Think about one contract interaction you build often — how would you verify not just state but the events and roles involved?

screens.title: Why test events?
screens.narratorSegment: Events are the primary way contracts communicate state changes to off-chain systems. When a contract emits an event, indexers, UIs, and backend services listen for that signal to update state, trigger notifications, or record history. Testing that an event is emitted with the correct arguments ensures those external systems receive reliable data. For example, a Counter contract that emits a CountChanged event provides the new count and caller address; if the event arguments are wrong, a front-end might display stale counts or misattribute actions. A common misconception is that testing state alone is enough. State checks verify internal storage, but they do not confirm the externally visible signal is correct. Another misconception is that events are optional; in practice they are part of your contract's public A P I when off-chain components depend on them. Concrete example: extend a simple Counter so increment and decrement emit CountChanged with the caller and new value. Then use to. emit and withArgs to assert both that the event fired and that its data matches expectations. Key takeaway: treat events as first-class outputs of contract behavior and assert them explicitly in tests.

keyIdea.title: Events are part of the external API
keyIdea.text: Always assert event emissions and arguments because off-chain consumers rely on them as much as they rely on on-chain state.

content.html:
Definition

Events as external signals

An event is a log that off-chain systems read. Tests must verify both that events fire and that their arguments match expected values.

Concrete Example
// contracts/CounterWithEvents.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract CounterWithEvents {
  uint public count;
  event CountChanged(address indexed caller, uint newCount, string message);

  constructor() { count = 0; }

  function increment() public {
    count++;
    emit CountChanged(msg.sender, count, "Incremented count");
  }

  function decrement() public {
    require(count > 0, "Count cannot go below zero");
    count--;
    emit CountChanged(msg.sender, count, "Decremented count");
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Events are essential outputs. Tests should check both emission and argument correctness to protect integrations.

Why this matters

From internal state to external contract API

  • State checks confirm storage; event checks confirm the messages your contract sends off-chain.
  • Indexers and front-ends subscribe to events rather than reading state continuously.
  • Event argument mismatches are a common integration failure mode when contracts evolve.
Misconception

Relying only on state assertions can hide problems where the event payload differs from the stored value. Always assert both when the event is part of the contract's external API.

screens.title: Asserting events with Waffle's to.emit and withArgs
screens.narratorSegment: Now let's translate event intent into concrete test assertions. Waffle's to. emit matcher checks that a transaction produced a specific event on a contract instance, and withArgs verifies the event payload. A typical test pattern deploys the contract in a beforeEach, then runs the transaction and asserts emission. For example, when the CounterWithEvents contract increments, you expect a CountChanged event with the caller's address and the new count value. The test uses the owner signer address for comparison. A misconception is to assert events by watching the transaction receipt manually; using matchers is clearer and fails when arguments differ. Another edge case is reverted transactions: a revert implies no successful event emission, so you assert the revert and avoid expecting events in the same call. Concrete test example below shows three test cases: increment emits withArgs, decrement emits withArgs after an increment, and decrement from zero reverts with the expected message. Read the test output carefully: when an expected event isn't emitted or arguments mismatch, the matcher yields a clear failure. Practicing this pattern will make integration with UIs and indexers dependable.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Event tests for CounterWithEvents

// test/CounterWithEvents.js
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("CounterWithEvents", function () {
  let CounterWithEvents, counter, owner, addr1;
  beforeEach(async function () {
    CounterWithEvents = await ethers.getContractFactory("CounterWithEvents");
    [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();
    counter = await CounterWithEvents.deploy();
    await counter.deployed();
  });

  it("Should emit a CountChanged event on increment", async function () {
    await expect(counter.increment())
      .to.emit(counter, "CountChanged")
      .withArgs(owner.address, 1, "Incremented count");
  });

  it("Should emit a CountChanged event on decrement", async function () {
    await counter.increment();
    await expect(counter.decrement())
      .to.emit(counter, "CountChanged")
      .withArgs(owner.address, 0, "Decremented count");
  });

  it("Should not emit an event if transaction reverts", async function () {
    await expect(counter.decrement()).to.be.revertedWith("Count cannot go below zero");
  });
});
Explanation
  • to.emit(contract, "Event") asserts the transaction produced the named event on that contract instance.
  • withArgs compares the event payload to expected values, including indexed addresses.
  • Reverted transactions should be asserted with revert matchers; they imply no successful emission.
Concrete advice

Always use the signer address you expect in withArgs and keep messages consistent. If you change the event signature, update tests immediately to prevent silent integration breakage.

Key Takeaway

Matcher-based tests make failures explicit: mismatched event arguments fail tests, protecting off-chain consumers.

screens.title: Integration tests: why and how
screens.narratorSegment: Integration tests exercise the real interactions between contracts to ensure composite behavior matches expectations. Consider a Token and a VendingMachine or TokenSale contract: the sale contract must hold tokens, a buyer must send Ether, the sale contract must transfer tokens to the buyer, and the Ether must accumulate in the sale contract. Unit tests of each contract do not verify the choreography between them. In integration tests you deploy both contracts in beforeEach, mint or transfer tokens to the sale contract, call approve if transfers use transferFrom, and then simulate a buyer sending Ether. You must check the buyer's token balance, the sale contract's token balance, and the sale contract's Ether balance after the purchase. Also assert that a TokensPurchased event is emitted with the correct buyer and amounts. A common pitfall is forgetting approvals or testing only happy paths; include insufficient funds and insufficient tokens tests. Integration tests mirror real deployments and expose approval and flow errors early. As a concrete planning step, sketch the sequence of actions, signers involved, expected state changes, and events you assert. This makes tests easier to write and reason about.

content.html:
Process Flow

Token sale integration scenario

1. Deploy
Deploy ERC20Token and TokenSale, setting price and passing token address.
2. Provision
Mint or transfer tokens to TokenSale and approve spending if needed.
3. Purchase
Buyer sends Ether to buyTokens, TokenSale transfers tokens and emits TokensPurchased.
Checks & assertions
  • Contract addresses and initial state are correct after deployment.
  • Buyer token balance increases, sale contract token balance decreases.
  • Sale contract's Ether balance increases by msg.value and a TokensPurchased event is emitted with correct arguments.
  • Edge cases: insufficient Ether, insufficient tokens, and approval failures are asserted and revert as expected.

content.html:
Starter: ERC20Token.sol
// contracts/ERC20Token.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract ERC20Token {
    string public name = "MyToken";
    string public symbol = "MTK";
    uint8 public decimals = 18;
    uint public totalSupply;

    mapping(address => uint) public balanceOf;
    mapping(address => mapping(address => uint)) public allowance;

    event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint value);
    event Approval(address indexed owner, address indexed spender, uint value);

    constructor(uint _initialSupply) {
        totalSupply = _initialSupply;
        balanceOf[msg.sender] = _initialSupply;
    }

    function transfer(address _to, uint _value) public returns (bool success) {
        require(balanceOf[msg.sender] >= _value, "Insufficient balance");
        balanceOf[msg.sender] -= _value;
        balanceOf[_to] += _value;
        emit Transfer(msg.sender, _to, _value);
        return true;
    }

    function approve(address _spender, uint _value) public returns (bool success) {
        allowance[msg.sender][_spender] = _value;
        emit Approval(msg.sender, _spender, _value);
        return true;
    }

    function transferFrom(address _from, address _to, uint _value) public returns (bool success) {
        require(balanceOf[_from] >= _value, "Insufficient balance");
        require(allowance[_from][msg.sender] >= _value, "Insufficient allowance");
        balanceOf[_from] -= _value;
        balanceOf[_to] += _value;
        allowance[_from][msg.sender] -= _value;
        emit Transfer(_from, _to, _value);
        return true;
    }
}

content.html:
Test Skeleton
// test/TokenSale.js (skeleton)
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("TokenSale integration", function () {
  let Token, token, TokenSale, tokenSale, owner, buyer;
  const TOKEN_PRICE = ethers.utils.parseUnits("1", "wei"); // example price in Wei

  beforeEach(async function () {
    Token = await ethers.getContractFactory("ERC20Token");
    TokenSale = await ethers.getContractFactory("TokenSale");
    [owner, buyer] = await ethers.getSigners();

    token = await Token.deploy(ethers.utils.parseUnits("1000", 18));
    await token.deployed();

    tokenSale = await TokenSale.deploy(token.address, TOKEN_PRICE);
    await tokenSale.deployed();

    // Arrange: transfer tokens to tokenSale so it can sell
    await token.transfer(tokenSale.address, ethers.utils.parseUnits("500", 18));
  });

  it("Deployment sets correct initial state", async function () {
    expect(await tokenSale.token()).to.equal(token.address);
    expect(await tokenSale.tokenPrice()).to.equal(TOKEN_PRICE);
  });

  // More tests: successful purchase, insufficient funds, insufficient tokens
});
Example assertion

A successful purchase test should assert the TokensPurchased event, buyer token balance increased by expected token amount, and tokenSale Ether balance increased by msg.value. Keep token amount calculations explicit so the test documents intent.

Pro Tip

Convert values using ethers.utils to avoid unit mistakes. Be explicit about decimals and tokenPrice units.

Common Mistake

Not transferring tokens into the sale contract during setup. Tests should arrange contract balances, not assume them.

screens.title: Simulating multiple users with signers
screens.narratorSegment: A powerful testing pattern is simulating multiple users with signers. Ethers provides signers that represent accounts; by default tests receive an array of ready-made signers. Use contract. connect(signer) to make calls as that account. This allows you to test buyer, owner, and attacker flows distinctly. For example, in a TokenSale test use owner to deploy contracts and transfer tokens to the sale contract, then use buyer to call buyTokens. If a transferFrom call is required, have the token owner call approve and then the buyer or sale contract execute the transferFrom as appropriate. A common error is calling functions with the wrong signer, which makes tests pass or fail for the wrong reason. Another subtle point is that addresses used in withArgs must match the signer. address used in the transaction. Concrete example: await tokenSale. connect(buyer). buyTokens({ value: buyValue }); then assert events include buyer. address. When testing permissioned functions, also simulate an unauthorized signer attempting the action and assert a revert. This pattern helps reveal permission bugs and ensures test coverage mirrors real-world actor interaction. Simulating multiple users with signers means use multiple signers and contract.connect to verify flows for owners, buyers, and potential attackers so roles behave as intended.. In practical terms, using ethers signers and contract.connect to represent different actors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Signers are role simulators
keyIdea.text: Use multiple signers and contract.connect to verify flows for owners, buyers, and potential attackers so roles behave as intended.

content.html:
Pattern

Simulating actors with signers

// Example usage
const [owner, buyer, attacker] = await ethers.getSigners();
// Deploy as owner
// Transfer tokens from owner to sale contract
await token.connect(owner).transfer(tokenSale.address, supply);
// Buyer purchases
await tokenSale.connect(buyer).buyTokens({ value: purchaseValue });
// Unauthorized actor tries admin action
await expect(tokenSale.connect(attacker).adminOnlyAction()).to.be.revertedWith("Not authorized");
Explanation
  • Use getSigners() to obtain accounts for tests and assign them roles by name in the test scope.
  • Always call contract.connect(signer) to make a transaction originate from that signer.
  • Match signer.address in withArgs to assert event payloads precisely.
Pro Tip

Name signers in beforeEach for clarity: owner, buyer, seller, attacker. Clear naming reduces accidental signer mixups.

screens.title: Hardhat Network essentials
screens.narratorSegment: Hardhat Network is a local Ethereum node built into Hardhat that runs when you execute test commands. Its speed and isolation make test runs fast and repeatable. Key capabilities that matter for advanced testing include console. log support from Solidity, impersonation of accounts, and direct manipulation of chain state such as increasing time or mining blocks. Console logging inside Solidity helps you print internal values during failing tests, which is invaluable for debugging complex logic. Impersonation lets you act as any account to simulate privileged actors or existing contract wallets without private keys. Time manipulation with evm_increaseTime and evm_mine lets you reproduce deadlines and locks deterministically. A misconception is to assume Hardhat exactly duplicates public testnets; it's a simulated environment optimized for testing logic. You should still run final checks on a public testnet before production. In practice, use Hardhat Network to iterate quickly and reproduce edge cases, and reserve public testnets for final integration and deployment verifications. Hardhat Network essentials means hardhat network provides console logging, impersonation, and time control so you can reproduce edge cases and debug solidity without testnet delays.. In practical terms, local blockchain features that speed development and debugging. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Hardhat Features
  • Speed & Isolation: Each test run gets a fresh, fast chain.
  • console.log in Solidity: Print values from contracts to the test log for debugging.
  • Impersonation: Act as any address to simulate privileged operations.
  • State control: Increase time or mine blocks to test time-dependent logic.
Example: console.log

You can add console.log calls in Solidity and see their output in the Hardhat test terminal. This is especially helpful for complex revert reasons or intermediate values in multi-contract flows.

Misconception

Hardhat Network is not a perfect replica of a public testnet. It's a simulation optimized for reproducible logic testing; final tests on public testnets remain important.

screens.title: Time manipulation in tests
screens.narratorSegment: Time-sensitive contracts require the ability to simulate the passage of time in tests. Hardhat Network supports evm_increaseTime to advance the chain clock and evm_mine to create a new block reflecting that time change. Use these together to test withdrawals after a lock period or vesting schedules. The pattern is simple: assert that an action reverts before the lock expires, increase time beyond the lock period, mine a block, and then assert the action succeeds. For example, a lockContract with a one-day lock will revert withdraw calls before time passes; after calling network. provider. send with evm_increaseTime of ONE_DAY_IN_SECS + 1 and then evm_mine, the withdraw call should succeed. Common mistakes include forgetting to mine a block after increasing time, which means the chain state hasn't updated, and choosing incorrect units when calculating seconds. Also remember that manipulating time changes every test's environment, so always perform time changes within a controlled test or beforeEach context to avoid cross-test interference. This technique makes testing time-dependent business logic deterministic and fast. Time manipulation in tests means use evm_increasetime and evm_mine to reproduce locks and deadlines without waiting in real time, then assert behavior before and after the change.. In practical terms, advance chain time and mine blocks to test locks and deadlines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Advance time deterministically
keyIdea.text: Use evm_increaseTime and evm_mine to reproduce locks and deadlines without waiting in real time, then assert behavior before and after the change.

content.html:
Time manipulation example
const { network } = require("hardhat");

it("Should allow withdrawal after time lock", async function () {
  const ONE_DAY_IN_SECS = 24 * 60 * 60;
  await expect(lockContract.withdraw()).to.be.revertedWith("Lock not expired");

  await network.provider.send("evm_increaseTime", [ONE_DAY_IN_SECS + 1]);
  await network.provider.send("evm_mine");

  await expect(lockContract.withdraw()).to.not.be.reverted;
});
Explanation & pitfalls
  • evm_increaseTime changes the internal timestamp; evm_mine creates a block using that new time.
  • Always mine a block after increasing time; without mining, tests won't see the updated block timestamp.
  • Use precise second calculations and document the time constants in tests for readability.
Pro Tip

Encapsulate time helpers in a test util so tests read clearly: fastForward(seconds) wrapping both calls reduces mistakes.

screens.title: Common testing mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Advanced tests can fail for predictable reasons. This checklist compares common mistakes against recommended practices. First, forgetting to arrange contract balances or approvals leads to failing purchases. Fix this by explicitly transferring tokens or calling approve in beforeEach. Second, not asserting events leaves the integration contract A P I unverified; always use to. emit and withArgs for event checks. Third, mixing signers or forgetting contract. connect(signer) can make tests pass incorrectly or cause unexpected reverts; name signers clearly and call connect for each actor. Fourth, ignoring time control causes flaky tests for locks; use evm_increaseTime and evm_mine within test scope. Fifth, relying solely on Hardhat without a final public testnet check assumes parity; use Hardhat for iteration but run final tests on a public testnet before production. For each mistake the remedy is a test pattern you can adopt: arrange state, assert events, simulate roles, control time, and perform final deployments to a public testnet. This comparison helps you build a test suite that is both thorough and maintainable. Common Mistake
Missing setup for token supply
Ensure TokenSale holds tokens or the tests transfer tokens during setup.

Include to.emit and withArgs to validate the contract's external signals.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how to test smart contract behavior beyond single-function unit checks. We'll focus on three practical areas: asserting event emissions so your front-end and indexers can rely on on-chain signals; building integration tests that exercise interactions between two or more contracts; and using Hardhat Network to simulate time, impersonate accounts, and debug with console logging. These capabilities help you catch bugs that unit tests miss: incorrect event arguments, approval mistakes, and time-dependent logic. You'll see concrete code examples: a Counter contract extended to emit events, Waffle assertions using the to. emit and withArgs matchers, and an integration test pattern for an ERC20 token and a TokenSale contract. We will also cover common mistakes like forgetting to use contract. connect(signer) or skipping event assertions. By the end, you'll understand how to structure tests that mirror real-world flows and how to use Hardhat's network features to reproduce scenarios that are hard to recreate on public testnets. Think about one contract interaction you build often — how would you verify not just state but the events and roles involved?

In this pair of objective screens you'll see the practical testing skills you'll master. First, you will implement event emission tests using Waffle's to. emit and withArgs matchers so you can assert that contracts broadcast the right signals and data. This matters because front-ends and indexers depend on those events. Second, you'll write integration tests that deploy and exercise multiple contracts together, verifying approvals, transfers, balances, and cross-contract events. Integration tests reveal bugs unit tests miss. Third, you'll learn to simulate different user roles in tests by using multiple signers and contract. connect(signer). This makes it possible to test permissioned flows, approvals, and attacks from other addresses. Finally, you'll use Hardhat Network for fast local execution, time manipulation, impersonation, and console logging to reproduce time-dependent scenarios and debug Solidity code. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint and a verified competency milestone to confirm you can run the corresponding test and explain the result.

This second objectives page focuses on deeper patterns that help when code and interactions grow complex. You will explore time manipulation to test locks, releases, and delays by advancing the chain clock and mining blocks. This is essential for contracts with time-locked withdrawals or staged vesting. You'll also learn to check that no events were emitted on reverted transactions by using revert assertions and understanding that a revert implies no successful emission. Events are the primary way contracts communicate state changes to off-chain systems. When a contract emits an event, indexers, UIs, and backend services listen for that signal to update state, trigger notifications, or record history. Testing that an event is emitted with the correct arguments ensures those external systems receive reliable data. For example, a Counter contract that emits a CountChanged event provides the new count and caller address; if the event arguments are wrong, a front-end might display stale counts or misattribute actions. A common misconception is that testing state alone is enough. State checks verify internal storage, but they do not confirm the externally visible signal is correct. Another misconception is that events are optional; in practice they are part of your contract's public A P I when off-chain components depend on them. Concrete example: extend a simple Counter so increment and decrement emit CountChanged with the caller and new value. Then use to. emit and withArgs to assert both that the event fired and that its data matches expectations. Key takeaway: treat events as first-class outputs of contract behavior and assert them explicitly in tests.

Now let's translate event intent into concrete test assertions. Waffle's to. emit matcher checks that a transaction produced a specific event on a contract instance, and withArgs verifies the event payload. A typical test pattern deploys the contract in a beforeEach, then runs the transaction and asserts emission. For example, when the CounterWithEvents contract increments, you expect a CountChanged event with the caller's address and the new count value. The test uses the owner signer address for comparison. A misconception is to assert events by watching the transaction receipt manually; using matchers is clearer and fails when arguments differ. Another edge case is reverted transactions: a revert implies no successful event emission, so you assert the revert and avoid expecting events in the same call. Concrete test example below shows three test cases: increment emits withArgs, decrement emits withArgs after an increment, and decrement from zero reverts with the expected message. Read the test output carefully: when an expected event isn't emitted or arguments mismatch, the matcher yields a clear failure. Practicing this pattern will make integration with UIs and indexers dependable.

Integration tests exercise the real interactions between contracts to ensure composite behavior matches expectations. Consider a Token and a VendingMachine or TokenSale contract: the sale contract must hold tokens, a buyer must send Ether, the sale contract must transfer tokens to the buyer, and the Ether must accumulate in the sale contract. Unit tests of each contract do not verify the choreography between them. In integration tests you deploy both contracts in beforeEach, mint or transfer tokens to the sale contract, call approve if transfers use transferFrom, and then simulate a buyer sending Ether. You must check the buyer's token balance, the sale contract's token balance, and the sale contract's Ether balance after the purchase. Also assert that a TokensPurchased event is emitted with the correct buyer and amounts. A common pitfall is forgetting approvals or testing only happy paths; include insufficient funds and insufficient tokens tests. Integration tests mirror real deployments and expose approval and flow errors early. As a concrete planning step, sketch the sequence of actions, signers involved, expected state changes, and events you assert. This makes tests easier to write and reason about.

A powerful testing pattern is simulating multiple users with signers. Ethers provides signers that represent accounts; by default tests receive an array of ready-made signers. Use contract. connect(signer) to make calls as that account. This allows you to test buyer, owner, and attacker flows distinctly. For example, in a TokenSale test use owner to deploy contracts and transfer tokens to the sale contract, then use buyer to call buyTokens. If a transferFrom call is required, have the token owner call approve and then the buyer or sale contract execute the transferFrom as appropriate. A common error is calling functions with the wrong signer, which makes tests pass or fail for the wrong reason. Another subtle point is that addresses used in withArgs must match the signer. address used in the transaction. Concrete example: await tokenSale. connect(buyer). buyTokens({ value: buyValue }); then assert events include buyer. address. When testing permissioned functions, also simulate an unauthorized signer attempting the action and assert a revert. This pattern helps reveal permission bugs and ensures test coverage mirrors real-world actor interaction. Hardhat Network is a local Ethereum node built into Hardhat that runs when you execute test commands. Its speed and isolation make test runs fast and repeatable. Key capabilities that matter for advanced testing include console. log support from Solidity, impersonation of accounts, and direct manipulation of chain state such as increasing time or mining blocks. Console logging inside Solidity helps you print internal values during failing tests, which is invaluable for debugging complex logic. Impersonation lets you act as any account to simulate privileged actors or existing contract wallets without private keys. Time manipulation with evm_increaseTime and evm_mine lets you reproduce deadlines and locks deterministically. A misconception is to assume Hardhat exactly duplicates public testnets; it's a simulated environment optimized for testing logic. You should still run final checks on a public testnet before production. In practice, use Hardhat Network to iterate quickly and reproduce edge cases, and reserve public testnets for final integration and deployment verifications. Time-sensitive contracts require the ability to simulate the passage of time in tests. Hardhat Network supports evm_increaseTime to advance the chain clock and evm_mine to create a new block reflecting that time change. Use these together to test withdrawals after a lock period or vesting schedules. The pattern is simple: assert that an action reverts before the lock expires, increase time beyond the lock period, mine a block, and then assert the action succeeds. For example, a lockContract with a one-day lock will revert withdraw calls before time passes; after calling network. provider. send with evm_increaseTime of ONE_DAY_IN_SECS + 1 and then evm_mine, the withdraw call should succeed. Common mistakes include forgetting to mine a block after increasing time, which means the chain state hasn't updated, and choosing incorrect units when calculating seconds. Also remember that manipulating time changes every test's environment, so always perform time changes within a controlled test or beforeEach context to avoid cross-test interference. This technique makes testing time-dependent business logic deterministic and fast. Advanced tests can fail for predictable reasons. This checklist compares common mistakes against recommended practices. First, forgetting to arrange contract balances or approvals leads to failing purchases. Fix this by explicitly transferring tokens or calling approve in beforeEach. Second, not asserting events leaves the integration contract A P I unverified; always use to. emit and withArgs for event checks. Third, mixing signers or forgetting contract. connect(signer) can make tests pass incorrectly or cause unexpected reverts; name signers clearly and call connect for each actor. Fourth, ignoring time control causes flaky tests for locks; use evm_increaseTime and evm_mine within test scope. Fifth, relying solely on Hardhat without a final public testnet check assumes parity; use Hardhat for iteration but run final tests on a public testnet before production. For each mistake the remedy is a test pattern you can adopt: arrange state, assert events, simulate roles, control time, and perform final deployments to a public testnet. This comparison helps you build a test suite that is both thorough and maintainable.
